cards.explanation: The answer is eats any food. Saul, Israel's king, put his troops under an oath: “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening…” (1 Samuel 14:24). That's a long day of fighting with nothing in the stomach. The text says the men were in distress, and I believe it. My mustache gets cranky after one skipped snack.

The answer is honey. The troops entered the forest, and “…there was honey on the ground.” (1 Samuel 14:25). Honey just lying out there for the taking, with an oath hanging over their heads. That's a tough spot for a hungry soldier, friends. I feel for them.

The answer is that they feared the oath. The text says it plainly: when they saw the flowing honey, not one of them put his hand to his mouth, “…because they feared the oath.” (1 Samuel 14:26). Saul's oath had real weight with them. They stayed hungry with the honey right there. That's some serious self-control, and I'm a little jealous.

The answer is False. Jonathan, Saul's son, did not leave the honey alone. He had not heard about the oath, so he dipped the end of his staff into the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth (1 Samuel 14:27). And his eyes brightened. The troops around him wouldn't touch the honey because they feared the oath (1 Samuel 14:26).

The answer is faint. A soldier tells Jonathan, Saul's son, “That is why the people are faint.” (1 Samuel 14:28). No food all day, and the fighting kept going. Faint is exactly the word, friends. Their strength was running low.

The answer is True. Jonathan, Saul's son, says, “My father has brought trouble to the land…” (1 Samuel 14:29). He says it right after the soldier tells him about the oath. He points to his own brightened eyes after a little honey. That's quite a thing to say about your own dad.

The answer is eaten freely from the plunder. Jonathan, Saul's son, says, “How much better it would have been if the troops had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies!” Then he asks, “Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?” (1 Samuel 14:30). In his view, fed troops fight better. Hard to argue with that.

The answer is that they eat meat with the blood still in it. The troops rushed greedily to the plunder, took sheep, cattle and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate meat with the blood still in it (1 Samuel 14:32). Someone then reported to Saul that the troops were sinning against the LORD (1 Samuel 14:33). Very faint men, a lot of meat, and no patience.

The answer is True. Saul says, “Each man must bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them in this place, and then eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.” (1 Samuel 14:34). Saul had asked for a large stone to be rolled over (1 Samuel 14:33). That night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.

The answer is an altar. Saul built an altar to the LORD. The text adds that it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). The troops had just slaughtered their oxen there (1 Samuel 14:34). That's a first worth noticing, friends.

The answer is consult God right there. The priest says, “We must consult God here.” (1 Samuel 14:36). Saul had just said let's go after the Philistines by night. The priest asked to stop and ask God first. Good call, and the right order.

The answer is False. God did not answer that same day. Saul asked God if he should go down after the Philistines and if God would give them into the hand of Israel, “But God did not answer him that day.” (1 Samuel 14:37). That's a quiet kind of day. And Saul's next move is to look into how this sin happened.

The answer is Jonathan. Saul says, “As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is Saul's son, and Saul names him before the lot is cast. The lot comes later, in verses 41 and 42. That's a big promise to make so early.

The answer is True. After Saul swears that whoever sinned must die, even his son Jonathan, “…not one of the troops said a word.” (1 Samuel 14:39). A whole army and total quiet. I think that's a heavy silence, friends.

The answer is Saul and Jonathan. Saul asked the LORD to answer with Urim if the fault was with him or Jonathan, and with Thummim if it was with the men of Israel. Then “…Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge.” (1 Samuel 14:41). So the people were cleared. The next step is a lot between the two of them.

The answer is False. The lot fell on Jonathan. After Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan.” the text says, “And Jonathan was selected.” (1 Samuel 14:42). Saul had sworn that whoever sinned must die, even if it was Jonathan. Now his son was the one selected.

The answer is that he swears Jonathan will surely die. Saul says, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” (1 Samuel 14:44). Jonathan had just told him he only tasted a little honey. Saul doubled down on his oath. That's a heavy part of the story.

The answer is that he brought a great deliverance for Israel. The people say, “Must Jonathan die…he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never!” (1 Samuel 14:45). They add, “…for with God’s help he has accomplished this today.” The troops finally speak up, friends. They point to what Jonathan did for Israel.

The answer is rescued. The text says, “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.” (1 Samuel 14:45). The troops had stayed silent earlier (1 Samuel 14:39). This time they spoke up, and it saved Jonathan. Good thing they found their voices.

The answer is that Saul gives up chasing them. The text says, “Then Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines…” (1 Samuel 14:46). Earlier he wanted to go down after them by night (1 Samuel 14:36). Now he stops. The Philistines went back to their own land. And the story isn't over, friends.
